variants.name: private/readonly modifiers and Readonly<T> (compile-time only)
variants.idiom_name: private readonly fields, constructor assignment, Readonly<T> holder
variants.implementation_notes: Parameter properties and `readonly` fields make the state assignable only in the constructor at the type level, and `Readonly<T>` plus `Object.freeze` give a frozen holder whose properties cannot be reassigned - the idiomatic TypeScript replacement for the Data class while the guarantee only needs to hold inside a type-checked codebase. The docs are explicit that `private` and `protected` are erased and enforced only during type checking, and `readonly` is not emitted as `writable: false`, so bracket notation, `in`, plain property lookup and any JavaScript consumer can still write the state. Use this variant for application code with a single build pipeline; switch to `#` private fields when the guarantee must survive compilation.
pitfalls: `private` and `protected` disappear in the emitted JavaScript, so runtime consumers can read and write those members (bracket notation, `in`, plain lookup) - never treat them as a security or integrity boundary.
`readonly` is a type-level constraint that TypeScript deliberately does not emit as `writable: false`, and `Object.freeze`/`Readonly<T>` are shallow, so nested data stays mutable.
Structural typing means a mutable twin of the class is assignable to the read-only type, so `readonly` does not stop a caller from holding the same instance through a mutable type.

variants.name: ECMAScript # private fields for hard privacy
variants.idiom_name: #data private field with getters (WeakMap-emulated below ES2015 targets)
variants.implementation_notes: Private fields written with `#` are ECMAScript, not TypeScript: the class body is the only place the name is legal, subclasses cannot see it, and the emitted code keeps the privacy at runtime - natively on modern targets, through WeakMap emulation when compiling to ES2021 or lower, which adds a lookup per access. Pair `#data` with getters (and `Object.freeze` on the holder) to get readable-but-not-writable state that survives compilation, which is the variant to choose for libraries and anything consumed by plain JavaScript. Note that `#` fields are invisible to `Object.keys`, `JSON.stringify` and `structuredClone`, so serialization must go through explicit methods.
pitfalls: Emitting `#` fields for ES2021 or older targets produces WeakMap-based emulation with an extra lookup per access, and the compiler cannot downlevel them at all below ES2015.

Private fields are not own properties, so `JSON.stringify`, `structuredClone`, spread and many mapping libraries silently skip them, and TypeScript forbids combining `#` with visibility modifiers or parameter properties.
A subclass declaring the same `#name` gets a different field rather than an override, so 'protected-like' sharing between a base class and its subclasses is impossible.
